content.markdown:
## Scenario context

Fluentd is an open-source data collector that decouples log sources from destinations. It ingests logs from 100+ sources (Nginx, Docker, syslog), normalizes them to JSON, applies filters and transformations, and routes them to 100+ outputs (Elasticsearch, S3, Kafka). Tag-based routing is the core concept.

---

Every piece of data flowing through Fluentd is called an **event**. Each event has exactly three component…

This walkthrough focuses on **Understanding Log Events: Tag, Time, and Record**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Every piece of data flowing through Fluentd is called an event .
- Each event has exactly three components: Think of it like a letter in a postal system: the tag is the address, the time is the postmark, and the record is the contents.
- Fluentd's routing engine reads only the tag to decide where the letter goes — it never needs to open the envelope.

**Concepts in play:** jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection, api-gateway, caching, database-indexing

## Stage 1 — Tags and Routing: Fluentd's Core Concept

- Every event in Fluentd has a tag — a dot-separated string that determines where the event is routed.
- - web.nginx events match <match web.
- → go to Elasticsearch - app.backend events match <match app.

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

```xml
<source>
  @type tail
  path /var/log/nginx/access.log
  tag web.nginx
  format nginx
</source>

<source>
  @type tail
  path /var/log/app/app.log
  tag app.backend
  format json
</source>

<match web.**>
  @type elasticsearch
  host elastic.local
  port 9200
  index_name nginx-logs
</match>

<match app.**>
  @type s3
  s3_bucket my-log-archive
  path logs/%Y/%m/%d/
</match>
```

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Nginx[Nginx access.log tag: web.nginx] --> Fluentd
    App[App log tag: app.backend] --> Fluentd
    Sys[Syslog tag: system.kernel] --> Fluentd

    Fluentd -->|match web.**| ES[Elasticsearch]
    Fluentd -->|match app.**| S3[Amazon S3]
    Fluentd -->|match system.**| Kafka[Kafka topic]
```

**Observable outcome:** → go to Elasticsearch - app.backend events match <match app.

## Stage 2 — End-to-End Pipeline: From Log Line to Storage

- Understanding the tag concept is one thing — seeing data flow from a raw log line all the way to a storage backend makes it concrete.
- The diagram below traces a single Nginx request through every stage of a typical Fluentd pipeline: Here is what happens at each step: 1.
- Input (tail) — Fluentd watches /var/log/nginx/access.log for new lines, stamping each with the tag web.nginx and a Unix timestamp.
- Parser (nginx) — The raw text line ( 127.0.0.1 - [date] "GET /api" 200 512 ) is parsed into a structured JSON record using Nginx's known log format.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

## Stage 3 — The Plugin Architecture: Input → Filter → Buffer → Output

- Fluentd's power comes from its plugin model: Buffer plugins are critical for reliability.
- Without buffering, a downstream outage (e.g., Elasticsearch restart) causes log loss.
- With a file buffer: - Events are written to disk first.
- - Flushed to the output on schedule (or when the buffer fills).

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

```architecture

  "version": 1,
  "title": "The Plugin Architecture: Input → Filter → Buffer → Output - Subsystem Overview",
  "description": "Decoupled system architecture isolating ingress, stateless logic, and persistent datastores.",

  "direction": "LR",

    { "id": "cache", "component": "redis", "label": "Redis Cache", "group": "data", "badge": "Sub-ms Reads" },
    { "id": "db", "component": "postgres", "label": "Transactional DB", "group": "data", "badge": "ACID Log" }
```

```xml
<match **>
  @type elasticsearch
  host elastic.local

  <buffer>
    @type file
    path /var/log/fluentd-buffer
    flush_interval 5s
    retry_max_times 10
  </buffer>
</match>
```

**Observable outcome:** - Flushed to the output on schedule (or when the buffer fills).

## Stage 4 — Deep Dive: Filter Enriching and Transforming Events

- Filters run in the pipeline between input and output: This adds environment , hostname , and a derived log level to every Nginx event before sending to Elasticsearch.

*Applies **database-indexing** to the decision above.*

```xml
<filter web.nginx>
  @type record_transformer
  enable_ruby true
  <record>
    environment "production"
    hostname "#{Socket.gethostname}"
    log_level ${record["status"].to_i >= 500 ? "ERROR" : "INFO"}
  </record>
</filter>
```

**Observable outcome:** Filters run in the pipeline between input and output: This adds environment , hostname , and a derived log level to every Nginx event before sending to Elasticsearch.

## Stage 5 — Practical: Collecting Kubernetes Container Logs

- In Kubernetes every container's stdout/stderr lands in /var/log/containers/ on the host node.
- A Fluentd DaemonSet reads these files and ships them to a central store.
- The ConfigMap below shows a minimal but production-ready pipeline: Three design decisions are worth calling out: - pos file records the last-read byte offset for every log file.
- If the Fluentd pod restarts (node eviction, OOM, rolling upgrade), it resumes from exactly where it left off — no duplicate lines, no gaps.

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

```yaml
# fluentd-configmap.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: fluentd-config
data:
  fluent.conf: |
    <source>
      @type tail
      path /var/log/containers/*.log
      pos_file /var/log/fluentd-containers.log.pos   # ← resume after restart
      tag kubernetes.*
      read_from_head true
      <parse>
        @type json
      </parse>
    </source>

    <filter kubernetes.**>
      @type kubernetes_metadata   # ← enriches with pod name, namespace, labels
    </filter>

    <match kubernetes.**>
      @type elasticsearch
      host "#{ENV['FLUENT_ELASTICSEARCH_HOST']}"
      port "#{ENV['FLUENT_ELASTICSEARCH_PORT']}"
      logstash_format true        # ← creates logstash-YYYY.MM.DD indices for Kibana
      logstash_prefix k8s
      <buffer>
        @type file
        path /var/log/fluentd-buffer
        flush_interval 5s
        retry_max_times 17
      </buffer>
    </match>
```

**Observable outcome:** If the Fluentd pod restarts (node eviction, OOM, rolling upgrade), it resumes from exactly where it left off — no duplicate lines, no gaps.

## Stage 6 — Logback Fluentd Appender: Shipping Structured Logs from Spring Boot to Fluentd

- Spring Boot applications log via SLF4J + Logback by default.
- The fluent-logger-java Logback appender encodes each log event as a MessagePack record and forwards it over TCP to Fluentd's @type forward input — the same Tag, Time, Record model described in this post.
- Structured field arguments (via logstash-logback-encoder ) become JSON keys in the Fluentd record, making them fully queryable in Kibana without any Fluentd filter plugin.
- The tag: app.payments in Logback maps directly to Fluentd's <match app.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

```xml
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.fluentd</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluent-logger</artifactId>
    <version>0.3.4</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>net.logstash.logback</groupId>
    <artifactId>logstash-logback-encoder</artifactId>
    <version>7.4</version>
</dependency>
```

```xml
<!-- src/main/resources/logback-spring.xml -->
<configuration>
    <!-- Console output for local development -->
    <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder"/>
    </appender>

    <!-- Fluentd forward appender for production -->
    <appender name="FLUENTD"
              class="org.fluentd.logger.logback.FluentLogbackAppender">
        <tag>app.payments</tag>           <!-- routes to <match app.**> in Fluentd -->
        <remoteHost>fluentd-aggregator</remoteHost>
        <port>24224</port>
        <maxQueueSize>500</maxQueueSize>  <!-- in-memory buffer before forward -->
    </appender>

    <springProfile name="prod">
        <root level="INFO">
            <appender-ref ref="FLUENTD"/>
        </root>
    </springProfile>
    <springProfile name="!prod">
        <root level="INFO">
            <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
        </root>
    </springProfile>
</configuration>
```

**Observable outcome:** The tag: app.payments in Logback maps directly to Fluentd's <match app.

footerPosts.title: Adapting to Virtual Threads for Spring Developers
footerPosts.subtitle: Migrate your Spring Boot services from thread-pool exhaustion to JDK 21 virtual threads — the practical Spring developer guide
footerPosts.brief: Platform threads (one OS thread per request) max out at a few hundred concurrent I/O-bound requests. Virtual threads (JDK 21+) allow millions — with zero I/O-blocking cost. Spring Boot 3.2 enables them with a single property. Avoid `synchronized` blocks wrapping I/O (they pin virtual threads to OS threads) and CPU-bound work inside virtual threads. For I/O-heavy Spring services, virtual threads are the most impactful JVM upgrade since Java 8 lambdas.

footerPosts.title: ACID Properties Explained: How SQL Databases Guarantee Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability
footerPosts.subtitle: From WAL and MVCC to fsync and isolation levels — the internals behind every ACID guarantee in PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, and SQL Server.
footerPosts.brief: ACID is four orthogonal guarantees that every SQL transaction must provide. Atomicity says all-or-nothing: PostgreSQL implements it via WAL rollback; MySQL InnoDB via undo logs. Consistency says constraints always hold: the database rejects any write that violates a `CHECK`, `FOREIGN KEY`, or `NOT NULL`. Isolation says concurrent transactions cannot see each other's intermediate states: PostgreSQL uses MVCC + Serializable Snapshot Isolation; MySQL InnoDB uses MVCC + Two-Phase Locking. Durability says committed data survives crashes: every major database writes to a write-ahead log and calls `fsync` before acknowledging a commit. Know which property protects which failure class — and know the configuration knobs that let you trade durability for throughput when the workload permits.

footerPosts.title: ACID Transactions in Distributed Databases: DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, and Spanner Compared
footerPosts.subtitle: How modern NoSQL databases achieve atomicity and isolation without a single machine
footerPosts.brief: ACID transactions in distributed databases are not equal. DynamoDB provides multi-item atomicity scoped to 25 items using two-phase commit with a coordinator item, but only within a single region. Cosmos DB wraps partition-scoped operations inside a stored procedure using a JavaScript continuation model — cross-partition writes get no atomic guarantee. Google Spanner is the only cloud database that delivers true global ACID with external consistency, using TrueTime (GPS + atomic clocks) to assign globally ordered timestamps and a commit-wait delay to guarantee causality across datacenters. MongoDB supports multi-document transactions on replica sets but carries measurable performance overhead and does not prevent write skew under snapshot isolation. The right choice depends on atomicity scope, latency tolerance, and operational cost — not on which database claims to be "ACID-compliant."

footerPosts.subtitle: Is an LLM a brain in a jar? To make it truly useful, we need to give it access to the world. This guide explains RAG and Agents.
footerPosts.brief: Large Language Models are brilliant "brains in a jar." Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) hands them a constantly refreshed memory, while AI Agents give them tools to act in the world. Combined, they turn static knowledge into dynamic, goal-directed intelligence — the next frontier of practical AI.

footerPosts.subtitle: Production AI needs explicit routing, memory, execution, and evaluation layers rather than one loop.
footerPosts.brief: A single agent loop is enough for a demo, but production AI systems need explicit layers for routing, execution, memory, and evaluation. Those layers determine safety, latency, cost, and traceability far more than model choice alone.

footerPosts.subtitle: Master shortest paths, dependency resolution, and cycle detection with robust Java solutions.
footerPosts.brief: Graph algorithms are the backbone of networking, scheduling, and connection analysis. This guide explores Dijkstra's pathfinding, Topological Sorting for dependency resolution, and Disjoint Set Union (DSU) for cycle detection, complete with runnable Java code.

footerPosts.title: AI Agents Explained: When LLMs Start Using Tools
footerPosts.subtitle: An LLM can talk, but an AI Agent can *act*. We explain how Agents use the ReAct framework to brow...
footerPosts.brief: A standard LLM is a brain in a jar — it can reason but cannot act. An **AI Agent** connects that brain to tools (web search, code execution, APIs). Instead of just answering a question, an agent executes a loop of Thought → Action → Observation until the goal is reached.

footerPosts.title: ANN Index Types Explained: When to Choose Flat, HNSW, IVF, or IVF-PQ
footerPosts.subtitle: A production-first guide to picking the right vector index for recall, latency, memory, and update patterns.
footerPosts.brief: If your dataset is small and correctness is critical, use Flat. If you need high recall with low latency and enough RAM, use HNSW. If your corpus is huge and memory is your bottleneck, use IVF-PQ. Start with HNSW for most RAG systems, then move to IVF or IVF-PQ when scale and cost force compression.

footerPosts.title: Apache Spark for Data Engineers: RDDs, DataFrames, and Structured Streaming
footerPosts.subtitle: Process petabytes with Python: understand Spark's execution model, DataFrame transformations, partitioning strategy, and real-time streaming.
footerPosts.brief: Apache Spark distributes Python DataFrame jobs across a cluster of executors, using lazy evaluation and the Catalyst query optimizer to process terabytes with the same code that works on gigabytes. Master partitioning, shuffle-awareness, and Structured Streaming and you have a single engine for both batch and real-time pipelines.

footerPosts.title: Attention Mechanism Explained: How Transformers Learn to Focus
footerPosts.subtitle: From the query-key-value formulation to multi-head attention — the mechanism that made transformers dominate AI
footerPosts.brief: Attention lets every token in a sequence ask "what else is relevant to me?" — dynamically weighting relationships across all positions simultaneously. It replaced the fixed-size hidden-state bottleneck of RNNs and is the engine behind every GPT, BERT, ViT, and AlphaFold model you have ever used.

footerPosts.title: API Gateway vs. Load Balancer vs. Reverse Proxy: What's the Difference?
footerPosts.subtitle: They all sit in front of your servers. But do you need Nginx, HAProxy, or Kong? We clarify the roles of each component.
footerPosts.brief: A **Reverse Proxy** hides your servers and handles caching/SSL. A **Load Balancer** spreads traffic across server instances. An **API Gateway** manages API concerns — auth, rate limiting, routing, and protocol translation. Modern tools (Nginx, AWS ALB, Kong) often combine all three, but understanding what each layer does independently is essential for system design.

footerPosts.title: Backend for Frontend (BFF): Tailoring APIs for UI
footerPosts.subtitle: Mobile apps need less data than Desktop dashboards. Why serve them the same JSON? The Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern solves this.
footerPosts.brief: A "one-size-fits-all" API causes bloated mobile payloads and underpowered desktop dashboards. The **Backend for Frontend (BFF)** pattern solves this by creating a dedicated API server for each client type — the mobile BFF reshapes data for small screens, the web BFF aggregates for dashboards.

footerPosts.title: BFS — Breadth-First Search: Level-by-Level Graph Exploration
footerPosts.subtitle: BFS explores graphs level by level using a queue — the key to shortest paths and level-order problems.
footerPosts.brief: BFS explores a graph level by level using a FIFO queue, guaranteeing the shortest path in unweighted graphs. Recognize BFS problems by keywords: "shortest path," "minimum steps," or "level order." Time: O(V + E). Space: O(V). Mark nodes visited on enqueue — never on dequeue.

footerPosts.title: Exploring Backtracking Techniques in Data Structures
footerPosts.subtitle: Backtracking is a brute-force algorithmic technique that solves problems by trying to build a sol...
footerPosts.brief: Backtracking is "Recursion with Undo." You try a path, explore it deeply, and if it fails, you **undo** your last decision and try the next option. It explores the full search space but prunes invalid branches early, making it far more efficient than brute force.

footerPosts.title: Big Data Architecture Patterns: Lambda, Kappa, CDC, Medallion, and Data Mesh
footerPosts.subtitle: Choose ingestion, serving, and ownership patterns deliberately when data platforms start to scale.
footerPosts.brief: A serious data platform is defined less by where files are stored and more by how changes enter the system, how serving layers are materialized, and who owns quality over time. Lambda, Kappa, CDC, Medallion, and Data Mesh are patterns for making those choices explicit.

footerPosts.title: Big Data 101: The 5 Vs, Ecosystem, and Why Scale Breaks Everything
footerPosts.subtitle: Why traditional databases fail at scale, what the 5 Vs really mean, and a practical map of the big data ecosystem from ingestion to insights.
footerPosts.brief: Traditional databases fail at big data scale for three concrete reasons — storage saturation, compute bottleneck, and write-lock contention. The 5 Vs (Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value) frame what makes data "big." A layered ecosystem — Kafka for ingestion, S3 for storage, Spark for processing, Snowflake for serving — assigns one tool per failure mode.

footerPosts.title: Exploring Different Types of Binary Trees
footerPosts.subtitle: Not all Binary Trees are created equal. We explain Full, Complete, Perfect, and Balanced Binary T...
footerPosts.brief: A Binary Tree has at most 2 children per node, but the **shape** of the tree determines performance. A **Full** tree has 0 or 2 children. A **Complete** tree fills left-to-right. A **Perfect** tree is a symmetric triangle. A **Degenerate** tree becomes a linked list with $O(N)$ search.

footerPosts.title: Big O Notation Explained: Time Complexity, Space Complexity, and Why They Matter in Interviews
footerPosts.subtitle: Master Big O notation: measure algorithm efficiency from O(1) to O(n²) with growth diagrams, worked examples, and the interview mental model.
footerPosts.brief: Big O notation describes how an algorithm's resource usage *grows* as input size grows — not how fast it runs on your laptop. Learn to identify the 7 complexity classes (O(1) through O(n!)), derive time and space complexity by counting loops and stack frames, and communicate your analysis in three sentences that satisfy any FAANG interviewer.

footerPosts.title: Binary Search Patterns: Five Variants Every Senior Engineer Knows
footerPosts.subtitle: Binary search has five distinct patterns — classic, leftmost, rightmost, rotated arrays, and 2D matrices.
footerPosts.brief: Binary search has five patterns beyond the classic "find the target": leftmost position, rightmost position, rotated array search, minimum in rotated array, and 2D matrix search. The root of every off-by-one bug is a mismatched loop condition and boundary update. Learn the invariant for each pattern and you will never write a broken binary search again.

morePosts.subtitle: ChatGPT isn't magic; it's math. We explain the core mechanism of Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPT) and how they predict the next word.
morePosts.brief: At its core, GPT asks one question, repeated: *"Given everything so far, what is the most likely next token?"* Tokens are not words — they're subword units. The Transformer architecture uses **self-attention** to weigh how much each token should influence the prediction. Sampling strategies (temperature, top-p) control how creative or deterministic the output is.

The key: instrument every prompt, capture every token, and alert on cost spikes before they hit your budget.

content.markdown:
## Scenario context

Fluentd is an open-source data collector that decouples log sources from destinations. It ingests logs from 100+ sources (Nginx, Docker, syslog), normalizes them to JSON, applies filters and transformations, and routes them to 100+ outputs (Elasticsearch, S3, Kafka). Tag-based routing is the core concept.

---

Every piece of data flowing through Fluentd is called an **event**. Each event has exactly three component…

This walkthrough focuses on **Understanding Log Events: Tag, Time, and Record**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Every piece of data flowing through Fluentd is called an event .
- Each event has exactly three components: Think of it like a letter in a postal system: the tag is the address, the time is the postmark, and the record is the contents.
- Fluentd's routing engine reads only the tag to decide where the letter goes — it never needs to open the envelope.

**Concepts in play:** jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection, api-gateway, caching, database-indexing

## Stage 1 — Tags and Routing: Fluentd's Core Concept

- Every event in Fluentd has a tag — a dot-separated string that determines where the event is routed.
- - web.nginx events match <match web.
- → go to Elasticsearch - app.backend events match <match app.

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

```xml
<source>
  @type tail
  path /var/log/nginx/access.log
  tag web.nginx
  format nginx
</source>

<source>
  @type tail
  path /var/log/app/app.log
  tag app.backend
  format json
</source>

<match web.**>
  @type elasticsearch
  host elastic.local
  port 9200
  index_name nginx-logs
</match>

<match app.**>
  @type s3
  s3_bucket my-log-archive
  path logs/%Y/%m/%d/
</match>
```

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Nginx[Nginx access.log tag: web.nginx] --> Fluentd
    App[App log tag: app.backend] --> Fluentd
    Sys[Syslog tag: system.kernel] --> Fluentd

    Fluentd -->|match web.**| ES[Elasticsearch]
    Fluentd -->|match app.**| S3[Amazon S3]
    Fluentd -->|match system.**| Kafka[Kafka topic]
```

**Observable outcome:** → go to Elasticsearch - app.backend events match <match app.

## Stage 2 — End-to-End Pipeline: From Log Line to Storage

- Understanding the tag concept is one thing — seeing data flow from a raw log line all the way to a storage backend makes it concrete.
- The diagram below traces a single Nginx request through every stage of a typical Fluentd pipeline: Here is what happens at each step: 1.
- Input (tail) — Fluentd watches /var/log/nginx/access.log for new lines, stamping each with the tag web.nginx and a Unix timestamp.
- Parser (nginx) — The raw text line ( 127.0.0.1 - [date] "GET /api" 200 512 ) is parsed into a structured JSON record using Nginx's known log format.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

```architecture
{
  "version": 1,
  "title": "End-to-End Pipeline: From Log Line to Storage - Storage Topology",
  "description": "Multi-tier caching and replicated storage pipeline ensuring fast reads and transactional consistency.",
  "view": "data-flow",
  "pattern": "cache-aside",
  "direction": "LR",
  "groups": [
    { "id": "compute", "label": "Application Workers", "tone": "blue" },
    { "id": "cache-tier", "label": "Volatile Memory Tier", "tone": "amber" },
    { "id": "storage-tier", "label": "Persistent Disk Tier", "tone": "green" }
  ],
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "worker", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Worker Process", "group": "compute" },
    { "id": "mem", "component": "redis", "label": "In-Memory Cache", "group": "cache-tier", "badge": "Hot Keys" },
    { "id": "primary", "component": "postgres", "label": "Primary Database", "group": "storage-tier", "badge": "Write Master" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "worker", "to": "mem", "kind": "read", "label": "Fast Read" },
    { "from": "worker", "to": "primary", "kind": "write", "label": "Transactional Commit" }
  ],
  "takeaway": {
    "title": "Storage Access Pattern",
    "body": "In-memory caching handles high-frequency read spikes, reserving disk transactions strictly for state modifications."
  }
}
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[ Nginx access.log] -->|tail plugin reads new lines| B[ Input: tail tag: web.nginx]
    B -->|raw text  JSON| C[ Parser: nginx {status, path, method}]
    C -->|add hostname + env fields| D[ Filter: record_transformer {status, path, hostname, env}]
    D -->|batch to disk first| E[ Buffer: file /var/log/fluentd-buffer]
    E -->|flush every 5 s| F[ Output: elasticsearch nginx-logs index]
```

**Observable outcome:** Parser (nginx) — The raw text line ( 127.0.0.1 - [date] "GET /api" 200 512 ) is parsed into a structured JSON record using Nginx's known log format.

## Stage 3 — The Plugin Architecture: Input → Filter → Buffer → Output

- Fluentd's power comes from its plugin model: Buffer plugins are critical for reliability.
- Without buffering, a downstream outage (e.g., Elasticsearch restart) causes log loss.
- With a file buffer: - Events are written to disk first.
- - Flushed to the output on schedule (or when the buffer fills).

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

```architecture
{
  "version": 1,
  "title": "The Plugin Architecture: Input → Filter → Buffer → Output - Subsystem Overview",
  "description": "Decoupled system architecture isolating ingress, stateless logic, and persistent datastores.",
  "view": "high-level",
  "pattern": "microservices",
  "direction": "LR",
  "groups": [
    { "id": "edge", "label": "Edge Traffic Ingress", "tone": "slate" },
    { "id": "services", "label": "Stateless Microservices", "tone": "blue" },
    { "id": "data", "label": "Datastore Infrastructure", "tone": "green" }
  ],
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "gw", "component": "api-gateway", "label": "API Gateway", "group": "edge", "badge": "TLS & Auth" },
    { "id": "app", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Domain Service", "group": "services", "badge": "Stateless" },
    { "id": "cache", "component": "redis", "label": "Redis Cache", "group": "data", "badge": "Sub-ms Reads" },
    { "id": "db", "component": "postgres", "label": "Transactional DB", "group": "data", "badge": "ACID Log" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "gw", "to": "app", "kind": "request", "label": "gRPC Request" },
    { "from": "app", "to": "cache", "kind": "read", "label": "Cache Lookups" },
    { "from": "app", "to": "db", "kind": "write", "label": "Durable Write" }
  ],
  "takeaway": {
    "title": "Architecture Boundary Invariant",
    "body": "Stateless compute nodes scale horizontally while shielding underlying database clusters behind fast cache layers."
  }
}
```

```xml
<match **>
  @type elasticsearch
  host elastic.local

  <buffer>
    @type file
    path /var/log/fluentd-buffer
    flush_interval 5s
    retry_max_times 10
  </buffer>
</match>
```

**Observable outcome:** - Flushed to the output on schedule (or when the buffer fills).

## Stage 4 — Deep Dive: Filter Enriching and Transforming Events

- Filters run in the pipeline between input and output: This adds environment , hostname , and a derived log level to every Nginx event before sending to Elasticsearch.

*Applies **database-indexing** to the decision above.*

```xml
<filter web.nginx>
  @type record_transformer
  enable_ruby true
  <record>
    environment "production"
    hostname "#{Socket.gethostname}"
    log_level ${record["status"].to_i >= 500 ? "ERROR" : "INFO"}
  </record>
</filter>
```

**Observable outcome:** Filters run in the pipeline between input and output: This adds environment , hostname , and a derived log level to every Nginx event before sending to Elasticsearch.

## Stage 5 — Practical: Collecting Kubernetes Container Logs

- In Kubernetes every container's stdout/stderr lands in /var/log/containers/ on the host node.
- A Fluentd DaemonSet reads these files and ships them to a central store.
- The ConfigMap below shows a minimal but production-ready pipeline: Three design decisions are worth calling out: - pos file records the last-read byte offset for every log file.
- If the Fluentd pod restarts (node eviction, OOM, rolling upgrade), it resumes from exactly where it left off — no duplicate lines, no gaps.

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

```yaml
# fluentd-configmap.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: fluentd-config
data:
  fluent.conf: |
    <source>
      @type tail
      path /var/log/containers/*.log
      pos_file /var/log/fluentd-containers.log.pos   # ← resume after restart
      tag kubernetes.*
      read_from_head true
      <parse>
        @type json
      </parse>
    </source>

    <filter kubernetes.**>
      @type kubernetes_metadata   # ← enriches with pod name, namespace, labels
    </filter>

    <match kubernetes.**>
      @type elasticsearch
      host "#{ENV['FLUENT_ELASTICSEARCH_HOST']}"
      port "#{ENV['FLUENT_ELASTICSEARCH_PORT']}"
      logstash_format true        # ← creates logstash-YYYY.MM.DD indices for Kibana
      logstash_prefix k8s
      <buffer>
        @type file
        path /var/log/fluentd-buffer
        flush_interval 5s
        retry_max_times 17
      </buffer>
    </match>
```

**Observable outcome:** If the Fluentd pod restarts (node eviction, OOM, rolling upgrade), it resumes from exactly where it left off — no duplicate lines, no gaps.

## Stage 6 — Logback Fluentd Appender: Shipping Structured Logs from Spring Boot to Fluentd

- Spring Boot applications log via SLF4J + Logback by default.
- The fluent-logger-java Logback appender encodes each log event as a MessagePack record and forwards it over TCP to Fluentd's @type forward input — the same Tag, Time, Record model described in this post.
- Structured field arguments (via logstash-logback-encoder ) become JSON keys in the Fluentd record, making them fully queryable in Kibana without any Fluentd filter plugin.
- The tag: app.payments in Logback maps directly to Fluentd's <match app.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

```xml
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.fluentd</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluent-logger</artifactId>
    <version>0.3.4</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>net.logstash.logback</groupId>
    <artifactId>logstash-logback-encoder</artifactId>
    <version>7.4</version>
</dependency>
```

```xml
<!-- src/main/resources/logback-spring.xml -->
<configuration>
    <!-- Console output for local development -->
    <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder"/>
    </appender>

    <!-- Fluentd forward appender for production -->
    <appender name="FLUENTD"
              class="org.fluentd.logger.logback.FluentLogbackAppender">
        <tag>app.payments</tag>           <!-- routes to <match app.**> in Fluentd -->
        <remoteHost>fluentd-aggregator</remoteHost>
        <port>24224</port>
        <maxQueueSize>500</maxQueueSize>  <!-- in-memory buffer before forward -->
    </appender>

    <springProfile name="prod">
        <root level="INFO">
            <appender-ref ref="FLUENTD"/>
        </root>
    </springProfile>
    <springProfile name="!prod">
        <root level="INFO">
            <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
        </root>
    </springProfile>
</configuration>
```

**Observable outcome:** The tag: app.payments in Logback maps directly to Fluentd's <match app.

## End-to-end outcome

Every piece of data flowing through Fluentd is called an event .

## Alternatives considered

### Real-World Applications: Fluentd vs Logstash vs Fluent Bit

The common production pattern: Fluent Bit as a lightweight DaemonSet on every node, forwarding to a central Fluentd aggregation layer, then to Elasticsearch/S3.

```yaml
      logstash_format true        # ← creates logstash-YYYY.MM.DD indices for Kibana
      logstash_prefix k8s
      <buffer>
        @type file
        path /var/log/fluentd-buffer
        flush_interval 5s
        retry_max_times 17
      </buffer>
    </match>
```

**Observable outcome:** If the Fluentd pod restarts (node eviction, OOM, rolling upgrade), it resumes from exactly where it left off — no duplicate lines, no gaps.

## Stage 6 — Logback Fluentd Appender: Shipping Structured Logs from Spring Boot to Fluentd

- Spring Boot applications log via SLF4J + Logback by default.
- The fluent-logger-java Logback appender encodes each log event as a MessagePack record and forwards it over TCP to Fluentd's @type forward input — the same Tag, Time, Record model described in this post.
- Structured field arguments (via logstash-logback-encoder ) become JSON keys in the Fluentd record, making them fully queryable in Kibana without any Fluentd filter plugin.
- The tag: app.payments in Logback maps directly to Fluentd's <match app.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

```xml
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.fluentd</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluent-logger</artifactId>
    <version>0.3.4</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>net.logstash.logback</groupId>
    <artifactId>logstash-logback-encoder</artifactId>
    <version>7.4</version>
</dependency>
```

```xml
<!-- src/main/resources/logback-spring.xml -->
<configuration>
    <!-- Console output for local development -->
    <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder"/>
    </appender>

    <!-- Fluentd forward appender for production -->
    <appender name="FLUENTD"
              class="org.fluentd.logger.logback.FluentLogbackAppender">
        <tag>app.payments</tag>           <!-- routes to <match app.**> in Fluentd -->
        <remoteHost>fluentd-aggregator</remoteHost>
        <port>24224</port>
        <maxQueueSize>500</maxQueueSize>  <!-- in-memory buffer before forward -->
    </appender>

    <springProfile name="prod">
        <root level="INFO">
            <appender-ref ref="FLUENTD"/>
        </root>
    </springProfile>
    <springProfile name="!prod">
        <root level="INFO">
            <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
        </root>
    </springProfile>
</configuration>
```

**Observable outcome:** The tag: app.payments in Logback maps directly to Fluentd's <match app.

It ingests logs from 100+ sources (Nginx, Docker, syslog), normalizes them to JSON, applies filters and transformations, and routes them to 100+ outputs (Elasticsearch, S3, Kafka).
Tag-based routing is the core concept.
